notes: Household size (v1.17.7): the table by household size changes only the number of people per flat (2 to 6). The roof tanks (2,592 m3), the treated-water tank, the membrane plant and the borewells are kept as set, so a smaller household leaves them larger than needed; the 648 m3 tank per flat building is 30 days of drinking-quality water at 5 persons per flat and lasts longer at 2 or 3.

Roof tank chambers (v1.17.8): each flat building has chamber A (pure water, the reserve) and chamber B (swing); the roof of the flat buildings fills A first (it is kept full), then B; the amenity tank fills from the amenity roof. Water for drinking and bathing is drawn from B first, then the amenity tank, then the reservoir, and chamber A last (it is the reserve). In the storm season (default September to November) chamber B is kept for storms: it is used first and is not topped up with pure water, so it is low when the heavy storms come; the space is the storm credit of the Net zero view. In the daily run it can still catch rain in the season, so the credit is not always whole: the heavy-rain-day table shows how much of the space is really free (about 63 % of all tank space on days of 64.5 mm or more, in the default case). The pure-water top-up fills the chambers outside the season and so raises the number of years in which water leaves the lease. With the pure-water top-up switch on, treated wastewater that would otherwise have no use (treated tank full) is passed through the membranes into A and then B. The dry-spell check starts with the roof tanks at their average content on 1 December from the daily run, not full. Overhead tanks, the flush chamber (it does not change the water balance, only shows its days of storage), the amenity building's own demand and first-flush loss are not modelled.

Closed loop: wastewater collected in the flats (80 % of use) goes through biological treatment with ultrafiltration (membrane bioreactor), then reverse osmosis and UV. 72 % of the domestic use is taken as the flow reaching the membrane plant; the remaining 28 % is use losses, sludge and treatment losses.

Reverse osmosis recovery is an assumption (75 %); the 25 % concentrate is led to toilet flushing first. It goes to irrigation only up to the share set in the inputs (default 0 %), so fresh-water plants and trees get treated wastewater, reservoir water or borewell water, not concentrate; the fountain never gets it. Its salt content is about four times that of the feed; a salinity and sodium check is needed before it is used anywhere, and flushing needs salt-tolerant fittings and its own pipe. Concentrate that finds no use is shown as concentrate with no use and needs an evaporation pond or another outlet, otherwise net zero is not met.

Priority each day (two grades): drinking-quality and bathing water from rain (roof tank, reservoir), then pure water, then borewell water (through reverse osmosis when that switch is on), then outside supply. Flushing, irrigation and the fountain: concentrate (flushing, then the allowed share of irrigation), treated wastewater, reservoir, borewell, outside supply. One grade: every use takes membrane-treated water and the concentrate has no use.

Borewell pumping capacity is a placeholder; there is no test pumping yet. The draft check compares the borewell water with the water the lease puts back: an assumed share (10 %) of rain on the open ground that soaks in, plus the water the reservoir sends down the recharge wells (v1.17.2; before this the recharge-well water was left out). The open-ground share is not measured.

Not yet linked to the other tabs (v1.17.2): the concentrate pond area is not taken out of the lease land in the Net Zero, Risk Calendar and Drought and Closed Loop runs, and its rain catch is not counted; the Net Zero 'water used from the reservoir after a storm' is typed by hand and is not the daily demand of the Closed Loop.

Singapore's NEWater is mostly used for industry and cooling and added to reservoirs in small, dry-season amounts before conventional treatment; direct supply of pure water for drinking in a housing project has no settled approval route in India. The option is shown separately so its value is visible.
Pure water from reverse osmosis has almost no minerals: remineralise (calcium, magnesium, alkalinity) and hold it in a tank with continuous monitoring before it enters the supply.

High-quality standard (v1.16.0, default): every litre used on the lease (flats, flushing, fountain, irrigation) must be high quality. Each day: rain (roof tank, reservoir; assumed treated by ultrafiltration and UV to the same standard, no loss), then pure water from the wastewater membranes, then borewell water passed through reverse osmosis, then outside supply. Nothing is given a lower-grade use, so all reverse osmosis concentrate (25 % of the membrane feed, from wastewater and from borewell water) has no use and must be kept on the lease (evaporation pond or other outlet) for net zero.

Borewell water: 3 borewells of about 1 L/s (3.6 m3/h) each, pumped 12 h/d, are a temporary placeholder taken from regional deep-borewell reports for Malur and Kolar (isolated deep fractures at 380 to 487 m yield 1 L/s or less; most ordinary bores 0.5 to 20 m3/h at 100 to 300 m). The block is over-exploited (stage about 179 to 180 %, water table below 80 m) and deep (Aquifer II) water often has fluoride and nitrate above the limits, so borewell water is passed through reverse osmosis. Test pumping and a water-quality test of the first borewell replace these figures.

Three-stage plan (v1.17.0): stage 1 pumps all the water from borewells; stage 2 adds the reuse of wastewater; stage 3 adds the reuse of rain. Borewell capacity is not limited in these three runs, so they show what the borewells would have to supply. Borewells needed = peak pumping day divided by what one borewell gives in a day (yield x pumping hours), rounded up. Pond area = concentrate divided by the net evaporation of the pond; the net evaporation is a placeholder until measured on site.
All numbers come from the 125-year IMD daily record and planner assumptions; none is calibrated on site.

Roof wetting: the one-storm sizing (net zero plan, one storm, season of storms) applies the roof coefficient to all the rain, with no wetting loss - the safe side for sizing the reservoir. The day-by-day views (risk calendar and drought, closed loop) take the first 1 mm of each rain day off the roof and the road before the coefficient - the safe side for supply. Over the 125-year record this gives about 13 % less roof water a year than no wetting loss.
